course_name_original: Máquinas Eléctricas para Generación y Tracción
course_name_en: Electrical Machines for Generation and Traction

learning_outcomes.text: Possess and understand knowledge that provides a basis or opportunity to be original in the development and/or application of ideas, often in a research context.
That students know how to apply the acquired knowledge and their problem-solving ability in new or little-known environments within broader (or multidisciplinary) contexts related to their area.

That students are able to integrate knowledge and face the complexity of formulating judgments based on incomplete or limited information, including reflections on social and ethical responsibilities linked to the application of their knowledge and judgments.
That students know how to communicate their conclusions and the ultimate knowledge and reasons that support them to specialized and non-specialized audiences in a clear and unambiguous way.
That students possess the learning skills that allow them to continue studying in a largely self-directed or autonomous way.
Understand the fundamental mathematical tools used in the analysis, modeling, and simulation of power systems.
Use computers and digital processors in general for the analysis, simulation, design, monitoring, control, and supervision of power systems.
Critically analyze data corresponding to the reading of the different magnitudes measured by the instrumentation subsystems.

Assess the risks of using electrical energy and, in general, of working in industrial facilities and using industrial equipment, understanding the need for safety elements, protection implementation, and signaling in power systems.
Manage both theoretically and practically the specific laboratory equipment for monitoring and control of power systems and electric vehicles.
Identify the aspects of technical design that depend most on strategic, socio-political, economic, and environmental conditions.
Understand the fundamental characteristics, as well as the advantages and limitations of electric and hybrid traction compared to combustion engines.
Acquire the power electronics knowledge necessary for the analysis and design of electric and hybrid traction systems.
Identify the participating agents in the electricity and gas market, as well as its operation considering different management methodologies.
Understand the price formation process, understanding the different components of the final price of electrical energy and tariffs.
Understand the importance and scope of use of electric power systems.
Know, characterize, and model the different primary energy sources and power loads.
Know the dynamic modeling of basic electric power systems.
Understand the operation, both in steady state and transient regime, of electrical machines used for generation and electric traction.
Compare electronic topologies and control methods that perform the same type of energy conversion and judge the most appropriate for each application.
Know the characteristics, the different design strategies, as well as the constructive elements and materials of electric power systems.
Understand the operating principle of electrical machines.
Know the different types of synchronous and asynchronous electrical machines used in generation and electric traction, their components, and their design and utilization criteria.
Identify the particular applications of each machine.

syllabus_topics: Fundamentals of electromechanical energy conversion in rotating electrical machines
General constructive analysis of electric machines
General concepts of three-phase rotating machine theory
Basic constructive aspects of three-phase asynchronous machines
Principle of operation of a three-phase asynchronous machine
Equivalent Circuit of a three-phase asynchronous machine
Influence of the design of the rotor in the mechanical characteristics
Control of reactive energy and torque
Features of permanent magnet synchronous machines
assessment_rules: To pass the ordinary examination, a minimum score of 4 out of 10 in the individual written exam (E) is mandatory, and class attendance must be at least 80%. If these conditions are met, the final grade is calculated as: (0.70 × E) + (0.20 × P) + (0.10 × A). Otherwise, the final grade will be the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. For extraordinary examinations, it consists of an individual written exam (EEX) and an individual project (PEX). A minimum score of 4 out of 10 in the individual written exam (EEX) is required. If this minimum is met, the final grade is calculated as: (0.70 × EEX) + (0.30 × PEX); otherwise, the final grade is the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0.
